DC-01.reason: Randomized experiments in two papers show herbicide increased native cover against no-herbicide plots in most site-years; only the 1996 cohorts showed no significant effect.

DC-02.reason: Randomized trials disagree: fertilization increased growth of black spruce, jack pine and white spruce in some studies, but had no effect on jack pine, tamarack, first-season height or height under scarification in others.

DC-03.reason: Several independent randomized studies with unscarified controls consistently report taller conifer seedlings after scarification (one null table row); the double- vs single-pass comparison doesn't address scarification vs none.

DC-04.reason: Quasi-experimental and longitudinal data from two sources show rewetting reduced tree cover/biomass and shrub biomass (vs non-rewetted sectors), though shrubs rebound over time; the 'prevents decreased tree dominance' encoding contradicts its sentence, which describes reversed canopy closure.

DC-05.reason: Two randomized studies with unlimed controls consistently report higher soil pH after liming.

DC-06.reason: Liming increased sugar maple sapling basal area and biomass but had no effect on beech growth, overall height or spruce height at most sites (one site positive).

DC-07.reason: A single before-after/reference quasi-experiment found water tables rose after ditch blocking in three of four transects, with no rise (or deepening) in the distant T23N transect.

DC-08.reason: One non-randomized grazed vs ungrazed marsh comparison found lower litter mass and lower end-of-season standing crop with grazing.

DC-09.reason: A single randomized study found lower exotic grass abundance with grass-specific herbicide, but only at one of its sites and compared with other disturbance treatments rather than an untreated control.

DC-10.reason: One randomized study found lower cover of several non-native species in burn treatments, but burning was combined with other actions (e.g. glyphosate) and some comparisons are against other treatments.

DC-11.reason: Before-after monitoring without controls found mostly no significant change in metal concentrations in crabs and sediment, but some years showed differences (Hg, Zn) and small decreases in sediment Cu and Hg.

DC-12.reason: Randomized studies in two papers found one-time mulch did not significantly affect native seedling density; the 'increased' edge's sentence is about exotic species changes and contradicts its encoding.

DC-13.reason: In one exclosure/observational study, browsed saplings generally had higher phenol and tannin levels than protected or lightly browsed saplings, with site exceptions.

DC-14.reason: One randomized study found weed removal increased seedling root collar diameter and biomass vs weed-intact plots, although effects varied by site and component.

DC-15.reason: Removing weeds increased conifer seedling diameter and biomass in a randomized study, implying competing vegetation reduces seedling growth (site-dependent).

DC-16.reason: The only edge's sentence compares browsing between species among unprotected trees, not sheltered vs unsheltered trees, so it says nothing about the shelter effect.

DC-17.reason: In a single exclosure study, sapling height was significantly greater inside than outside moose exclosures.

DC-18.reason: A randomized study found exponentially fertilized seedlings had greater height, root collar diameter and biomass than conventionally fertilized seedlings at both sites in some years.

DC-19.reason: Mulch had only a borderline, non-significant effect (p = 0.06) on species assemblages, and only on one date.

DC-20.reason: A cross-sectional chronosequence found soil exchangeable K stayed relatively stable after forest was converted to fallow fields.

DC-21.reason: Movement models show bears moving toward, away from, or indifferent to seismic lines depending on sex, season, land cover and line vegetation height.

DC-22.reason: One randomized study with unlimed controls found base saturation 1.4 to 3.3 times higher in limed soils at both depths.

DC-23.reason: Liming increased sugar maple sapling basal area and biomass growth but had no effect on American beech growth or overall height growth.

DC-29.reason: The only edge says fertilization strengthened scarification's effect on GLD, which is moderation, not fertilization's own effect on GLD.

DC-30.reason: In a randomized trial, total basal area was highest in uncut controls and lower in all cutting treatments; the other edges cover subsets (high-quality stock, sawlog AGS) rather than total basal area.

DC-31.reason: All edges describe scarification x cutting or scarification x year interactions or comparisons among scarification types, not a main effect of scarification on seedling density.
